body: {"total":5,"records":[{"title":"Clinically indicated replacement of peripheral intravenous catheters in adults: a systematic review of catheter failure, phlebitis and bloodstream infection","authors":"Delacroix-Mensah L, Nakamura-Pike J, Oduya-Fraser C, Brennan-Soto R","year":2021,"venue":"Nursing Evidence Syntheses","doi":"10.5555/nes.2021.0306","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We searched five databases to June 2020 for trials and cohort studies comparing clinically indicated with routine replacement of peripheral intravenous catheters in adults. The review included 9 trials and 11 cohort studies. In the trials, phlebitis and bloodstream infection did not differ between the two strategies, and clinically indicated replacement led to fewer insertions per patient. The cohort studies reported more variable results: catheter failure was higher after a policy change in 3 of 11. Few studies accounted for patients who had several catheters, and most cohort studies did not adjust for changes in patient mix over time."},{"title":"Peripheral catheter-associated bloodstream infection by dwell time in adult inpatients: a surveillance cohort from six hospitals","authors":"Rutherford-Mbeki A, Kowalczyk-Obi D, Tanaka-Holm E","year":2019,"venue":"Infection Surveillance Reports","doi":"10.5555/isr.2019.0072","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"Six hospitals reported peripheral catheter-associated bloodstream infections through a shared surveillance system for three years, covering about 214,000 peripheral catheters. The infection rate was 0.08 per 1,000 catheter-days overall. Rates were similar for catheters in place up to 96 hours and for catheters in place longer, but catheters inserted in the emergency department had about twice the rate of catheters inserted on the wards. Staphylococcus aureus caused most infections. Only 58 infections occurred in total, so the estimates by dwell time were imprecise, and the hospitals used different replacement policies during the period."},{"title":"Accounting for several catheters per patient in analyses of peripheral intravenous catheter failure: a methodological case study","authors":"Varela-Achterberg N, Holt-Adeyemi S","year":2024,"venue":"Clinical Nursing Evidence Letters","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"Using 6,120 peripheral catheters from 2,874 adult admissions, we compared analyses of catheter failure that treated catheters as independent with analyses that accounted for several catheters per patient. The analysis that ignored clustering gave a hazard ratio of 1.24 for dwell beyond 96 hours, with a 95 percent confidence interval of 1.08 to 1.42, while a shared frailty model gave 1.12, with an interval of 0.93 to 1.35. Patients with many catheters were sicker and contributed a disproportionate share of failures. We recommend patient-level clustering in every analysis of catheter failure and reporting the number of catheters per patient."},{"title":"Removal reasons for peripheral intravenous catheters in the electronic flowsheet: completeness and agreement with bedside observation","authors":"Pike-Oduya R, Lindholm-Varga E","year":2016,"venue":"Clinical Documentation in Nursing","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We compared the removal reason recorded in the electronic flowsheet with the reason observed by a research nurse at the bedside for 540 peripheral catheter removals on four wards. A removal reason was missing for 11 percent of removals. Where a reason was recorded, it agreed with the observed reason for 86 percent of removals; disagreement was most common between infiltration and occlusion and between end of treatment and dislodgement. Removals on night shifts more often lacked a reason. We recommend a fixed list of removal reasons and a check of free-text entries before any analysis of catheter failure."},{"title":"Nursing time for peripheral catheter care before and after a change to clinically indicated replacement: a time-motion study","authors":"Linwood-Okafor J, Castellanos-Moreau D","year":2023,"venue":"Ward Nursing Outcomes Quarterly","doi":"10.5555/wnoq.2023.0019","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"Trained observers timed peripheral catheter tasks on two medical wards for four weeks before and four weeks after a change from routine resiting to clinically indicated replacement. Time spent on insertions fell from 41 to 26 minutes per 10 patients per day, while time spent on site assessment and documentation rose from 12 to 19 minutes. Nurses reported fewer difficult insertions at night. The study did not measure catheter complications, and the observers knew which period they were observing, which may have influenced the timings."}]}
